title: Thoreau's limits
hook: critics call him prickly and self-righteous, and his friends sometimes agreed

segments.voice: Yesterday, no quarrel: Thoreau's reported answer that he didn't know he and God had ever quarreled. Did you drop one fight, even for a breath? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

After Thoreau died, Emerson wrote a long tribute to him. Emerson was his friend. And right in the middle of the praise, he slips in a sentence that sounds almost like a complaint: "It cost him nothing to say No; indeed he found it much easier than to say Yes." That's a friend talking, in a tribute meant to honor him. Not an enemy. We've spent weeks with Thoreau's best lines. Today, honestly, the other side.
screen: `EMERSON'S TRIBUTE.` → `EASIER TO SAY NO.` → `THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the no. Emerson says it plainly: refusal came easily to Thoreau. That's the same quality that sent him to jail rather than pay a tax he found unjust. It's also the quality that could make him hard to be around. Second, the elm tree. Emerson passes on a line from one of Thoreau's friends. I love Henry, the friend said, "but I cannot like him; and as for taking his arm, I should as soon think of taking the arm of an elm-tree." Love, yes. Ease, no. He was upright, rooted, and not soft to lean on. Third, the huckleberry party. Emerson counts it a fault that Thoreau had no ambition. He thought Thoreau had the gifts to lead great public work, and instead, he writes, "Instead of engineering for all America, he was the captain of a huckleberry-party." Some readers hear that as a put-down. Others hear quiet praise in it: he chose to lead friends to the berries. Fourth, the critics. Some readers since then have found Thoreau preachy, scornful of his neighbors, quick to judge how others lived while he lived so differently. Those are fair things to notice. His books do scold. But notice what Emerson does with all this. He names the prickles, and then keeps praising. The tribute holds both. A person can be hard to like and still be good, and still be worth learning from. That may be what Thoreau's friends teach best about him.
screen: `EASIER TO SAY NO.` · `THE ARM OF AN ELM TREE.` · `CAPTAIN OF A HUCKLEBERRY PARTY.` · then, large: `HARD TO LIKE, STILL GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love one prickly person. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is hard to like. Not someone who harms you. Just someone sharp, stubborn, quick to say no. Picture them clearly, prickles and all. Name one prickle honestly. Then, like Emerson, name one thing that is good in them, something real. Hold both at once, the way a friend held Thoreau: love without pretending it's easy. The bell holds the time.
Thoreau's limits. The prickly side his own friends named, and loved him through. Today's word.
Your line: prickly and good. Today, when someone's sharp edge catches you, look for the good thing standing right next to it. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.
